clue.text: Put forward in favour of sterling

parts.note: pro is Latin for 'for', used in English to mean in favour of
the pound is the unit of British sterling currency

explanation.surface: Someone argues the case for keeping the British currency.
explanation.definitionFit: To propound a theory is to offer or propose it for consideration.

clue.text: Fruit is lying ready for the barrow boys

parts.note: a pear is a fruit
lies means is lying, telling untruths or reclining

explanation.surface: A costermonger's fruit is laid out waiting for the street traders.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrow boys are London street traders selling from carts; their festive dress is covered with mother-of-pearl buttons, as worn by the Pearly Kings and Queens.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearlies are the pearl buttons and button-covered costumes traditionally worn by London costermongers.

clue.text: In shape for the premiere of Henry the Fifth

definitions.text: In shape for the premiere of Henry the Fifth

parts.words: In shape for the premiere of Henry the Fifth
parts.note: Shakespeare's Henry V was first staged in the round Globe theatre, which its prologue calls 'this wooden O'

explanation.walkthrough: 'In shape' suggests being fit for opening night; it means the shape of the playhouse, the circular Globe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Globe was a circular theatre, round like a ball or ring.

clue.text: Beds left-bank bird ?

parts.note: Beds is short for Bedfordshire, whose county town Bedford stands on the river Ouse
L is the abbreviation for left, set on the river's bank beside its name

explanation.surface: A bird seen on the left bank of a river in Bedfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedfordshire, abbreviated Beds, is an English county crossed by the Great Ouse; 'Beds' also hints at river beds.
explanation.definitionFit: The ousel is the blackbird, or the related ring ouzel and water ouzel, a songbird.

clue.text: Dined in Le Nid — most elegant!

indicators.note: the word for eating goes inside the word for the bird's home

parts.note: le nid is French for the nest
dined means ate

explanation.surface: A diner praises the stylish French restaurant Le Nid.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Nid looks like a restaurant name, but it is simply French for 'the nest'.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat can mean smart and tidy, so the superlative means trimmest or most stylish.

clue.text: King that Lear was

explanation.surface: A question about which monarch Shakespeare's Lear really was.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Shakespeare's King Lear, but the Lear meant is the nonsense poet Edward Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward is the name of eight English kings, and it was also the first name of the limerick writer Lear.

clue.text: Not even upset about sinning — that was bold

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for sinning is surrounded
upset in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read from the bottom

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd
erring means sinning, going astray

explanation.surface: Doing wrong without a care is praised as daring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even' suggests 'not even upset' in the surface, but it is the word for an uneven number; in a down clue 'upset' turns it bottom to top, and 'about' makes it the outside of the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Derring-do means daring deeds, heroic action of the kind that was brave.

clue.text: An aperitif nationally distinguished to a girl

parts.note: It is short for Italian vermouth, an aperitif named for its nation, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: A man offers a woman a drink with a strong national character.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'gin and It' is gin with Italian vermouth; the drink's name marks it out by its country.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita is a woman's first name.

clue.text: Right jacket for this work

parts.note: a heavy workman's coat and drudgery share one animal's name, so that name fits both jacket and work

explanation.walkthrough: A donkey jacket is the thick coat worn by British labourers, and donkey work is hard, dull toil.
explanation.definitionFit: The beast of burden names both the labourer's coat and heavy drudgery.

clue.text: Live a rustic not abreast of things

parts.note: to be is to live, to exist
a hind is an old word for a farm labourer

explanation.surface: Living like a yokel leaves one out of touch with events.
explanation.definitionFit: Being late or lagging means not keeping up with developments.

clue.text: Plan to waylay morning trans-sport procession

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning hours
a coinage on the pattern of motorcade and cavalcade: a parade of buses, the bus being a means of transport

explanation.surface: Someone plots to hold up an early-morning parade of vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trans-sport' is a pun on transport; a 'buscade' is an invented word, a procession of buses on the model of motorcade.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambuscade is an old word for an ambush, a plan to lie in wait and attack.

clue.text: One of the shortest was five eighth's'

definitions.text: One of the shortest was five eighth's

parts.words: One of the shortest was five eighth's
parts.note: follows on from 5 across: the times on the throne of Edward the Fifth and Edward the Eighth were among the shortest of English monarchs

explanation.walkthrough: Edward V ruled for about two months in 1483 and Edward VIII for under a year in 1936 before abdicating; the clue leans on 5 across, EDWARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period on the throne is his rule, and those two Edwards had very brief ones.

clue.text: It's not far to this " health " resort

definitions.text: It's not far to this " health " resort

parts.words: It's not far to this " health " resort
parts.note: the nearby pub, where people drink to each other's health with a toast

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain one's nearest pub is called the local; 'health' is in quotes because the toast 'Good health!' is drunk there, not because it is a spa.
explanation.definitionFit: The neighbourhood pub is a short walk away and is where drinkers raise glasses to good health.

clue.text: What some heat processes do

parts.note: heats are preliminary rounds of a race, which knock out the slower competitors

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heat processes' suggests chemistry or metallurgy, but a heat here is a qualifying round in athletics.
explanation.definitionFit: Qualifying heats remove the losers from the competition, getting rid of them.

clue.text: One fish makes another look aggrieved

parts.note: the eel is a snake-like fish
to pout is to push out the lips in sulky resentment

explanation.surface: One fish pulls a sulky face at a second fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An eelpout is a kind of marine fish with an eel-like body, so it is a different species of fish.

clue.text: Sounds cooling to a head in the red

indicators.note: sounds signals that the letters entered are a word pronounced the same as another phrase

parts.note: a draught over one's head cools it

explanation.surface: An overheated person in debt is told to cool their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Draught and draft are said alike, so 'over draught' (air blowing over the head) gives the banking word.
explanation.definitionFit: An overdraft is money owed to a bank on a current account, the state of being in debit.

clue.text: Unembarrassed by an unspeakable joke in current Scots

indicators.note: the joke sits inside the river's name, splitting it after its second letter

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, a current flowing through Aberdeen
a gag is both a joke and something that stops a person speaking

explanation.surface: Someone stays unruffled by a dirty joke told among Scots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current Scots' looks like 'present-day Scottish people' but means a Scottish river; 'unspeakable' points to the second sense of gag, a mouth-stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: Dégagé is a French loan meaning relaxed and free of awkwardness, at ease.

clue.text: Depressed area with Dot and Owen

parts.note: a glen is a narrow valley, a low-lying area
dot is an old word, from French, for a dowry, a bride's portion, as is dower

explanation.surface: A gloomy region shared by a woman named Dot and a man named Owen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dot' looks like a woman's name but is the old word for a dowry. Owen Glendower (Owain Glyndŵr) was the Welsh prince who rebelled against Henry IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen was the first name of the medieval Welsh leader in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1.

clue.text: Yet bread can be given away

indicators.note: can be means the letters may be made into something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A loaf might still be donated.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret that is given away has been disclosed or let out treacherously.

clue.text: Religious ally

definitions.meaning: a member of the Society of ..., the Quakers, is called a ...
an ally is someone on your side, a comrade

explanation.surface: A churchgoer who is on one's side.
explanation.definitionFit: Quakers call one another Friends, and a supporter or companion is also a friend.

clue.text: Several dippy types

definitions.meaning: an old word meaning several or various
people who dip under water, plungers

explanation.surface: A handful of scatty people.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means various, and the noun names people who plunge into water.

clue.text: Ward in favour of East-End mutton

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a teg is a sheep in its second year, a source of mutton
E is the abbreviation for East, put at the end

explanation.surface: A child in care backs the meat of London's poorer East End.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is London's traditional working-class district; here 'East-End' instead tells you to put E (East) at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A protégé is someone under the guidance and protection of a patron, much as a ward is under a guardian.

clue.text: Dad poorly clad is looked up to

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father
with a rag on, wearing rags, is shabbily dressed

explanation.surface: A father in shabby clothes is still respected.
explanation.walkthrough: Read RAGON as 'rag on', wearing a rag, for poorly clad.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a model of excellence, someone admired and esteemed by others.

clue.text: An 8 is one Italian town

parts.note: the answer to 8 down is a beast of burden, also called an ass
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A beast of burden is said to be a whole Italian town.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to 8 down, whose beast is an ass. Assisi is the Umbrian hill town of St Francis.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria in central Italy.

clue.text: He goes to bed nude

parts.note: the bed is the sea bed, and 'nude' describes diving without a suit or breathing gear

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about sleeping naked; the bed is the floor of the sea and the bare skin is the swimmer's.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who swims underwater wearing little and without a bulky suit goes down to the sea floor.

clue.text: Winter-sweet

parts.note: both frost forming in cold weather and the sugary coating of a cake

explanation.walkthrough: Wintersweet is a real shrub, which misleads; the two halves describe frost forming and the sugar on a cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Frost forming on surfaces in cold weather and a cake's sugar topping share this word.

clue.text: Arnold thought it a perch for a nightingale

definitions.text: Arnold thought it a perch for a nightingale

parts.words: Arnold thought it a perch for a nightingale
parts.note: in Matthew Arnold's poem Philomela the nightingale sings from a tree on an English lawn

explanation.walkthrough: Matthew Arnold's Philomela speaks of the bird singing from 'that wild, unquiet breast' among the trees of an English lawn, where the tree named is a cedar.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem places the singing bird in this evergreen conifer on a moonlit lawn.

clue.text: Song to please the field

definitions.meaning: a round for several voices, often a comic one
in cricket the fielding side is delighted when a fielder takes the ball before it bounces

explanation.surface: A tune sung to delight the fielders.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket 'the field' is the fielding team; a caught ball dismisses the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch is a round sung by several voices, and also the taking of a hit ball before it lands, which dismisses a batter.

clue.text: I have pop business at a popular resort

parts.note: biz is the slangy, popular shortening of business, as in showbiz

explanation.surface: A promoter boasts of running a music venture at a busy holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' suggests pop music but means colloquial: BIZ is the slang form of business.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is a Spanish Balearic island much visited by holidaymakers.

clue.text: Get off on the wrong foot, Tommy, at once

definitions.text: Get off on the wrong foot, Tommy
definitions.meaning: Tommy is a British private soldier, who steps off on the left foot; going away on the right one is wrong for him

explanation.surface: A sergeant tells a soldier who starts marching out of step to fix it immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy (Tommy Atkins) is slang for a British soldier; drill demands the left foot first, so moving off on the right is the wrong foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting off with the right foot is a march begun wrongly, and the phrase also means immediately.

clue.text: Mint variety of stingo

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters of stingo take another arrangement

explanation.surface: A distiller describes a minty version of a strong old ale.
explanation.walkthrough: Stingo is an old word for strong beer; 'Mint' looks like a flavour but is the place where bars of gold are made.
explanation.definitionFit: Bars of cast metal are produced and stored by a mint, the place that makes money.

clue.text: Held to bed

parts.note: a ship held fast to the sea bed by its heavy hook

explanation.walkthrough: 'Held to bed' suggests an invalid confined to bed; the bed is the sea floor, gripped by a ship's hook.
explanation.definitionFit: A moored vessel is fixed to the seabed by the weight dropped on a chain.
